## The idea

How uncertain is a coin flip? A die roll? Tomorrow's weather, or the party that wins the next election? Claude Shannon's information entropy puts a number on uncertainty: the average surprise of an outcome, measured in bits. A fair coin has one bit; a two-headed coin has zero; a fair eight-sided die has three. Entropy is the only measure of uncertainty that satisfies a few natural requirements, which is why it appears everywhere from data compression to ecology.

Page uses entropy as a lens for classifying processes. Stephen Wolfram sorted the outcomes of systems into four classes: **equilibrium** (nothing changes), **periodic** (a fixed cycle), **random** and **complex** (structured but not repetitive). Computing entropy over longer and longer blocks of a sequence separates them: equilibrium has zero entropy, cycles have low entropy that stops growing, random sequences have the maximum, and complex ones lie in between. Entropy also guides modelling assumptions: if all we know is a range, a mean, or a mean and variance, the distributions that assume nothing more are the uniform, the exponential and the normal.

## Formulation

::: {.model-box}
**Information entropy.** For a probability distribution $(p_1, \dots, p_N)$,

$$
H_2(p_1, \dots, p_N) = -\sum_{i=1}^{N} p_i \log_2 p_i ,
$$

maximized by the uniform distribution ($H_2 = \log_2 N$) and zero when one outcome is certain.

**Block entropy.** For a sequence of symbols, let $p(b)$ be the frequency of each block $b$ of $k$ consecutive symbols. Then $H_k = -\sum_b p(b)\log_2 p(b)$, and $h_k = H_k - H_{k-1}$ is the new uncertainty each additional symbol brings.

**Results.**

- Classification: equilibrium has $H_k = 0$; a cycle of period $m$ has $H_k$ that stops growing at $\log_2 m$; a random binary sequence has $H_k = k$ bits; a complex sequence grows more slowly than $k$ without levelling off.
- Maximum entropy: given only a range $[a, b]$ the maximum-entropy distribution is uniform; given a mean $\mu$, exponential; given a mean and variance, normal.
:::

Shannon's measure is the unique one (up to the base of the logarithm) satisfying four axioms: it is continuous in the probabilities, it is largest for equally likely outcomes, adding impossible outcomes leaves it unchanged, and the uncertainty of a two-stage outcome is the uncertainty of the first stage plus the expected uncertainty of the second.

## Interactive model

Choose a source of binary sequences. The strip shows the first 120 symbols; the chart shows block entropy $H_k$ for blocks of 1 to 8 symbols against the random benchmark (the diagonal). The presidential-election sequence, the winning party in each election from 1868 to 2016, is Page's example: its entropy is close to that of a random sequence of the same length.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
import {rng, range, entropy, C, fmt} from "../js/models.js"
```

```{ojs}
viewof source = Inputs.select(["Fair coin (random)", "Biased coin", "Sticky (repeats with probability q)", "Complex (rule 110 automaton)", "Periodic (ABBABB…)", "Equilibrium (AAAA…)", "US presidential elections, 1868–2016"], {value: "Sticky (repeats with probability q)", label: "Source"})
viewof q = Inputs.range([0.5, 0.99], {value: 0.85, step: 0.01, label: "Bias or stickiness q"})
viewof seed = Inputs.range([1, 500], {value: 25, step: 1, label: "Random seed"})
```

```{ojs}
seqData = {
  const r = rng(seed), L = 2000;
  if (source === "US presidential elections, 1868–2016") return [..."RRRRDRDRRRRDDRRRDDDDDRRDDRRDRRRDDRRDDR"].map(c => (c === "R" ? 1 : 0));
  if (source === "Equilibrium (AAAA…)") return new Array(L).fill(0);
  if (source === "Periodic (ABBABB…)") return range(L).map(i => (i % 3 === 0 ? 0 : 1));
  if (source === "Fair coin (random)") return range(L).map(() => r.bernoulli(0.5));
  if (source === "Biased coin") return range(L).map(() => r.bernoulli(q));
  if (source === "Sticky (repeats with probability q)") {
    const s = [r.bernoulli(0.5)];
    for (let i = 1; i < L; i++) s.push(r() < q ? s[i - 1] : 1 - s[i - 1]);
    return s;
  }
  // Rule 110: one cell's history in a wrapped row of 400 cells.
  const W = 400;
  let row = range(W).map(() => r.bernoulli(0.5));
  const out = [];
  for (let t = 0; t < L + 200; t++) {
    if (t >= 200) out.push(row[W / 2]);
    row = row.map((c, i) => (110 >> ((row[(i - 1 + W) % W] << 2) | (c << 1) | row[(i + 1) % W])) & 1);
  }
  return out;
}
```

```{ojs}
blocks = range(8).map(i => {
  const k = i + 1, counts = new Map();
  for (let j = 0; j + k <= seqData.length; j++) {
    const b = seqData.slice(j, j + k).join("");
    counts.set(b, (counts.get(b) || 0) + 1);
  }
  const total = seqData.length - k + 1;
  return {k, H: total > 0 ? entropy([...counts.values()].map(c => c / total)) : NaN, distinct: counts.size};
})
```

```{ojs}
Plot.plot({
  ariaLabel: "Information Entropy: the first symbols of the sequence",

})
```

```{ojs}
Plot.plot({
  ariaLabel: "Information Entropy: block entropy by block length",
  ariaDescription: "Horizontal axis: block length k from 1 to 8. Vertical axis: block entropy in bits. The teal line is the chosen sequence; the dashed diagonal is a perfectly random binary sequence. The summary below the charts states the result in words.",
  height: 260,

  marks: [
    Plot.line([[1, 1], [8, 8]], {stroke: "currentColor", strokeDasharray: "4 3", strokeOpacity: 0.6}),

})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
```
```{.js}
{
  const H1 = blocks[0].H, H4 = blocks[3].H, H8 = blocks[7].H, rate = blocks[7].H - blocks[6].H;
  const cls = H1 < 0.01 ? "**equilibrium**: there is no uncertainty at all"
    : rate < 0.05 ? "**periodic**: entropy stops growing once blocks span the cycle"
    : rate > 0.9 ? "**random**: each new symbol adds almost a full bit of surprise"
    : "neither cyclic nor random: entropy keeps growing, but more slowly than a coin's, the mark of structure (a **complex** or correlated process)";
  return html`<div class="sim-readout">${md`For ${seqData.length} symbols, the entropy of single symbols is **${fmt(H1, 2)} bits**, of blocks of four **${fmt(H4, 2)} bits** (a fair coin gives 4), and of blocks of eight ${fmt(H8, 2)} bits. ${source.startsWith("US") ? "With only 38 elections, long blocks are rare, so the block entropy is capped by the sequence's length; Page reports that the sequence is statistically indistinguishable from random." : `The last symbol added ${fmt(rate, 2)} bits: this looks ${cls}.`}`}</div>`;
}
```

## R {.unlisted}

```{.r}
# Information entropy and block entropies of binary sequences.
q <- 0.85 # stickiness: chance of repeating the last symbol
len <- 2000
set.seed(25)

entropy2 <- function(p) -sum(p[p > 0] * log2(p[p > 0]))
block_entropy <- function(x, k) {
  blocks <- sapply(1:(length(x) - k + 1), function(j) {
    paste(x[j:(j + k - 1)], collapse = "")
  })
  entropy2(table(blocks) / length(blocks))
}

sticky <- numeric(len)
sticky[1] <- rbinom(1, 1, 0.5)
for (i in 2:len) {
  sticky[i] <- if (runif(1) < q) sticky[i - 1] else 1 - sticky[i - 1]
}
sources <- list(
  random = rbinom(len, 1, 0.5),
  sticky = sticky,
  periodic = rep(c(0, 1, 1), length.out = len),
  elections = as.integer(strsplit(chartr(
    "RD", "10",
    "RRRRDRDRRRRDDRRRDDDDDRRDDRRDRRRDDRRDDR"
  ), "")[[1]])
)
h <- sapply(sources, function(x) sapply(1:8, function(k) block_entropy(x, k)))
print(round(h, 2))

matplot(1:8, h,
  type = "b", pch = 19, lty = 1,
  col = c("grey50", "#148a91", "#d95f02", "#7570b3"),
  xlab = "Block length k", ylab = "Block entropy (bits)"
)
abline(0, 1, lty = 2)
```

:::

## Takeaways

::: takeaways
- Entropy is the average surprise of an outcome, in bits; it is maximal when all outcomes are equally likely.
- Block entropies separate equilibrium, periodic, random and complex processes; the last two need care to tell apart.
- When we know only a range, a mean or a variance, the maximum-entropy distribution is the honest default.
:::

## Uses

::: uses
- **Explain.** Classify time series (heartbeats, markets, elections, hat choices) as ordered, cyclic, random or complex.
- **Reason.** Justify uniform, exponential or normal assumptions as the least informative ones consistent with what we know.
- **Predict.** Low-entropy processes are predictable; maximal entropy means no model of the past will help.
:::
